data.title: Seborrhoeic keratosis — viva
data.summary: Benign tumours & cysts · 10 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Seborrhoeic keratosis** (Benign tumours & cysts)_

**Q1. What is seborrhoeic keratosis (SK)?**
- Commonest benign epidermal tumour of middle-aged and elderly; well-demarcated, 'stuck-on', verrucous, waxy, light-brown to black papules/plaques on trunk, face, scalp, limbs (not palms/soles); FGFR3 and PIK3CA activating mutations; familial tendency

**Q2. Clinical variants.**
- Common, reticulated (adenoid), irritated/inflamed, clonal, dermatosis papulosa nigra (multiple small dark papules on face of dark-skinned people — very common in India, from adolescence), stucco keratosis (grey-white keratotic papules on ankles/legs of elderly), melanoacanthoma, inverted follicular keratosis, flat SK (resembles solar lentigo)

**Q3. Dermoscopy.**
- Comedo-like openings, milia-like cysts, cerebriform (brain-like) pattern with fissures and ridges ('fat fingers'), hairpin vessels with white halo, sharp moth-eaten border, network-like structures

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Exophytic acanthotic proliferation of basaloid keratinocytes above the level of surrounding epidermis ('string sign'), horn cysts and pseudo-horn cysts, papillomatosis, variable melanin
- Types: acanthotic (commonest), hyperkeratotic, reticulated, clonal (Borst–Jadassohn phenomenon — intraepidermal nests), irritated (squamous eddies), melanoacanthoma

**Q5. Write short notes on Borst–Jadassohn phenomenon (PYQ).**
- Intraepidermal nests of morphologically distinct cells within the epidermis — 'intraepidermal epithelioma'; seen in clonal SK, hidroacanthoma simplex (intraepidermal poroma), Bowen's disease (clonal), Paget's disease, melanoma in situ

**Q6. What is the sign of Leser–Trélat?**
- Sudden eruption of multiple SKs or rapid increase in size/number — paraneoplastic sign of internal malignancy (GI adenocarcinoma — stomach, colon; lymphoma), often with malignant AN and pruritus; also reported with erythroderma, pregnancy, HIV, drugs (cytarabine — inflamed SKs)

**Q7. Differential diagnosis.**
- Melanoma (especially pigmented, irritated SK), pigmented BCC, solar lentigo, melanocytic naevus, wart, AK, SCC (irritated SK), dermatosis papulosa nigra vs skin tags/syringomas

**Q8. Treatment.**
- Reassurance — benign, no malignant potential
- Removal for irritation, cosmetic reasons or diagnostic doubt: cryotherapy, curettage (± light cautery), shave excision, electrodesiccation/radiofrequency, CO2/Er:YAG laser, TCA application; topical hydrogen peroxide 40% (FDA approved)
- Dermatosis papulosa nigra: light electrodesiccation/curettage, scissor snip, lasers — caution for PIH in dark skin
- Biopsy if any doubt (melanoma)

**Q9. What is the genetic basis of SK?**
- Somatic activating mutations of FGFR3 (≈ 40–50%) and PIK3CA, also RAS; age and UV-related; not malignant (benign clonal neoplasm)

**Q10. What is dermatosis papulosa nigra?**
- Variant of SK in darker skin (Africans, Indians): multiple small dark-brown/black papules on malar face, forehead, neck from adolescence; familial; treated (cosmetic) with light electrodesiccation, curettage, scissor snip, lasers — risk of pigmentary change

## Quick spotter facts
- Stuck-on waxy verrucous plaque with milia-like cysts and comedo-like openings — SK
- Sudden eruption of SKs — Leser–Trélat

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Benign epidermal tumours). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
